subtopic: EXPRESSIONS OF FELICITATIONS ON THE OCCASION OF HIS BIRTHDAY

speechtext:
Mr. NORMAN J. M. LOCKHART (Lincoln) : Mr. Speaker, I rise to speak to a matter of privilege affecting one member of the House of Commons in particular, and for that purpose I crave your indulgence for a few moments.
A person is usually known by the company he keeps. May I be permitted to refer to an item which appeared in the Montreal Gazette of yesterday, April 13, and which concerns in particular the hon. member to whom I have referred. The names of the three illustrious persons mentioned in the Gazette were His Excellency the Earl of Athlone, the former Governor General of Canada; the Honourable Walter Jones, Premier of Prince Edward Island, and-no less important than the other two-none other than our genial vice-chairman of the committee of the whole, the hon. member for Huron-Perth (Mr. Golding). These three names are linked together, and rightly so.
It was reported in the Gazette that these illustrious persons are today passing another milestone in their journey through life. Before stating my question of privilege I consulted the Parliamentary Guide and found to my amazement that our genial friend from Huron-Perth has inadvertently omitted from that record the date of his birth. I traced his career to earlier days and I found that April 14 was his natal day.
I express my appreciation, sir, of your indulgence in allowing me to discuss the matter at this time. What I am saying was prompted particularly by consultation with the hon. member for Kingston City (Mr. Kidd), whom, I might say, very little passes. I feel sure that every hon. member in the chamber will join with the hon. member for Kingston City and me in conveying to our genial friend the felicitations of all members of the House of Commons, and that all will join with us in wishing him many happy returns on this his natal day, and many more years of preference and distinction.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, before the motion is carried I should like to make an observation. For a quarter of a century the banking and commerce committee has been convened in an orderly way so that members of the committee would find it convenient to be present when the committee was called. My reason for rising at this time is to say that in the mail box of members of the committee there was found, some time after the hour of ten o'clock in the morning, a notice saying that the banking and commerce committee would meet, while the house was in session, at 8.30 that day.
Those who open their mail boxes before ten o'clock in the morning and not again until later in the evening find themselves bereft of the information that this long-established committee on banking and commerce, which meets ordinarily when the house is in session, is to be convened on that day. As a member
Questions

of this house I am of opinion that there is ample time and ample opportunity for those who order the convening of the committee to give notice of it in the ordinary way so that the itinerary for our march during the day may be so arranged that we shall be able to attend its meetings.
Yesterday through no fault of his the member for Danforth innocently stood to one side while the committee on banking and commerce was being convened, and in his innocent sort of way he knew not thereof. This committee has been functioning since confederation, and with so much time now being available for our meetings, a notice given after 10 o'clock in the morning that we shall meet at 8.30 o'clock that day while the house is sitting is not sufficient for the old-fashioned representatives who still sit in this honourable assembly.
Motion agreed to.

1.	Since entering upon his duties as Secretary of State for External Affairs, has the Right Honourable Louis St. Laurent met (a) official representatives of the government of Soviet Russia; (b) official representatives of countries other than Russia?

Mr. ST. LAURENT: I should like to answer this question orally. First, with respect to representatives of governments other than Russia, the answer to that question is yes. In answer to the second question I should like to say that it is not in accordance with diplomatic practice nor in the national interest to disclose the nature of official conversations with representatives of other countries.
With respect to the representatives of Soviet Russia, the answer will have to be somewhat
qualified in order to be accurate. Since I assumed my duties as Secretary of State for External Affairs there has been no occasion for official conversations between representatives of Soviet Russia and the Secretary of State for External Affairs. As hon. members know, the post of ambassador from Russia to this government has not been filled, and such conversations as there may have been would be conversations between the charge d'affaires or members of his staff and members of the permanent staff of the department.
On the other hand it would not be accurate to say that I had not met any representatives of the Russian government. No doubt I participated in meetings of the united nations where there were representatives of that government, and I have no doubt it did happen that I attended social functions where they were also present. Those were the only times when I had occasion to meet them since I assumed the duties of my office.

He said: Mr. Speaker, this is the usual annual motion to set up the committee on railways and shipping which deals with the affairs of the Canadian National Railways and Trans-Canada Air Lines, and to which is referred the annual reports of the Canadian National Railways, the Canadian National (West Indies) Steamships, and Trans-Canada Air Lines. maintopic: RAILWAYS AND SHIPPING
subtopic: APPOINTMENT OF COMMITTEE ON ACCOUNTS AND ESTIMATES OF GOVERNMENT OWNED TRANSPORTATION LINES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I would have thought that the minister would not have brought in this motion until after the amendment moved by the leader of the C.C.F. party to the motion for supply had been disposed of. It has been thirty years since we have had a revision of the Railway Act, the last revision being in 1919. There have been vast changes since then. There have been very few results, so far as I have observed, from the setting up of this committee each year. The accounts are referred to the committee, which makes a report but concurrence in the report is not moved, and that is the last we hear of it. It means that the House of Commons is simply divesting itself of all control over the Canadian National Railways and its ocean, hotel and lake services. If you ask me, we have got very little value from this committee, and certainly this motion should have stood until the amendment of the hon. member for Rosetown-Biggar (Mr. Coldwell) had been disposed of.
I do not believe in the setting up of this committee at all. It is not the proper way in which to conduct the business of the house. Here is the annual report of the Canadian National Railways, in a booklet with these flowery pictures on the covers, and it shows a deficit of $23,000,000 on last year's operations. Who is going to pay that deficit? It is charged very largely to consolidated revenue fund, which means that the two central provinces of Ontario and Quebec are paying 74 per cent of all these deficits. We have no control over
rates or over the money the railways are spending on the system, on hotels, on ocean services and subsidiaries. Thirty years ago the province of Prince Edward Island sent up an old boat, the Northumberland, to be used on lake Ontario by the Canadian National subsidiary, but on two occasions the hon. member for Davenport (Mr. MacNicol) instead of going with his picnic to Port Dal-housie on such a boat as that, went in safety to Centre Island.
I can tell you this: too much is charged up to capital expenditures on the system which should be charged against earnings. Furthermore the refunding system is all wrong. Talk about subsidiaries; we cannot get a steam suburban service in the Toronto district, although Montreal has had one for thirty years. The headquarters of this national railways should be moved back to the public-ownership city where it started with the old Grand Trunk, in Toronto, and made all its money. They scrapped the old Grand Trunk in Ontario and used the funds to build the Grand Trunk Pacific from Moncton to Winnipeg.
I am opposed to the principle of this motion, for the reasons I have given. The capital structure is all wrong. The forgotten people are the taxpayers of Ontario and Quebec, who have to make up these deficits. The committee might just as well never meet. The time has come to revise the whole set-up of this system. Handouts of passes should be abolished and the British system of paying cash for everybody adopted instead. The board of transport commissioners has not been consulted on these various reports. It is all done over their heads. The Drayton-Acworth report set out wrhat should be done with this government-owned railway, and how to avoid deficits. There is too much interference. The committee might just as well never meet because it has done nothing but whitewashing ever since it started.
Motion agreed to.

speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I would like to direct a question to the government. Has it refused to grant an interview to representatives of the Housewives Consumers Association? maintopic: HOUSEWIVES CONSUMERS ASSOCIATION
subtopic: QUESTION AS TO INTERVIEW WITH MEMBERS OP GOVERNMENT
speechtext:
Perhaps I might answer that
question, Mr. Speaker. Representatives of the Housewives Consumers Association have visited me on I think at least two occasions, perhaps three, and on each occasion some of my colleagues were present. I came to the conclusion, as they did, that the primary purpose of these delegations was to foster communist propaganda. I am quite aware, as my hon. friend the member for Rosetown-Biggar (Mr. Coldwell) has indicated, that a great many people who come with these delegations and form part of the association are not communists nor do they support communist propaganda. Nevertheless I came to the conclusion that that is what these delegations were being used for. One of the leading spokesmen in the last delegation who took an active part in the discussion was a well-known communist from the city of Toronto.
For these reasons the government felt it was not justified in facilitating movements of that kind. The advice that was given to these organizations was that the government would be prepared to consider any representa-

tions which they cared to make in writing, but was not prepared to facilitate mass demonstrations of this kind in Ottawa.

maintopic: HOUSEWIVES CONSUMERS ASSOCIATION

I do not think it is the duty of myself, or of any of the ministers, to facilitate that sort of propaganda, and that is the reason why we refused them.

maintopic: HOUSEWIVES CONSUMERS ASSOCIATION

speechtext:
The house resumed from Tuesday, April 13, consideration of the motion of Mr. Abbott, for committee of supply, and the amendment thereto of Mr. Coldwell, and the amendment to the amendment of Mr. Bracken.
Mr. GORDON B. ISNOR (Halifax): Mr. Speaker, on April 5 the hon member for Rose-town-Biggar (Mr. Coldwell) rose in his place and asked leave to move the adjournment of the house for the purpose of discussing a definite matter of urgent public importance, namely, the proposed increases in freight rates authorized by the board of transport commissioners, which rates it is understood to be posted by the railroads concerned on April 8. Having received permission, the hon. member proceeded to present 'to the house a very reasonable and well thought out argument.

maintopic: FREIGHT RATES-INCREASES ORDERED BY TRANSPORT BOARD-AMENDMENT, MR. COLDWELL- SUBAMENDMENT, MR. BRACKEN
speechtext: Less noise in the house.

maintopic: FREIGHT RATES-INCREASES ORDERED BY TRANSPORT BOARD-AMENDMENT, MR. COLDWELL- SUBAMENDMENT, MR. BRACKEN
speechtext: Thank you.

maintopic: FREIGHT RATES-INCREASES ORDERED BY TRANSPORT BOARD-AMENDMENT, MR. COLDWELL- SUBAMENDMENT, MR. BRACKEN
speechtext: Order.

maintopic: FREIGHT RATES-INCREASES ORDERED BY TRANSPORT BOARD-AMENDMENT, MR. COLDWELL- SUBAMENDMENT, MR. BRACKEN
speechtext:
Again I say, as I have said in the past, that the hon. member for Peel is always considerate, and apparently he is anxious to hear what I have to say. I appreciate his kind consideration.
I was saying that the hon. member for Rosetown-Biggar proceeded to present a very reasonable and well thought out argument as to why he did not believe that the decision of the board of transport commissioners was one which would be well received in all sections in Canada. After he had presented his case he was followed by other members representing the different parties, and together with two other members from Nova Scotia I had an opportunity at that time of taking part in debate.
While I do not wish to go over the ground which was then covered, I do wish to refer to certain remarks I made on that occasion, because of the amendment by order in council which was later introduced by the Minister of Transport.
At that time I did not have the report of the Canadian National Railways, although I did point out that it was difficult for those residing in the maritime provinces to understand why a 30 per cent increase in freight rates was necessary, in view of the large increase in revenue in 1947 over 1946, particularly in connection with freight operations. Since then I have received a copy of the annual report of the Canadian National Railways, and it is shown that 78-2 per cent of the total revenue of the railway company was derived from freight rates. That 78-2 per cent in 1947 represented $342,582,002 as against $300,313,198 from the same source in 1946, an increase of $42,268,803 in the freight receipts. It was also shown in the report that there was a decrease in the passenger traffic, represented in dollars and cents, amounting to $7,110,000. I mention that figure because, in the summing up of the case by the board of transport commissioners in their finding, they took the whole operation into consideration.
I should like also to point out that there was an increase in the express rates. Whereas in 1946 the receipts for express were $19,579,478, in 1947 they had increased to $21,251,783, am increase for the year of $1,672,304. Therefore it was a little difficult at the time this decision was made for the man in the street to understand why this increase was granted.
It is true the application made by the two railways was for an increase of 30 per cent, and having received representations from the

Freight Rates
various provinces and parties throughout the dominion, they decided that 21 per cent was all that was necessary.
Representations were made from seven of the nine provinces. It was mentioned on one occasion, as something rather strange to those living in other parts of Canada than Ontario and Quebec, that these two provinces did not make representations. Well, I believe the other sections of Canada know the reason. These provinces were not greatly concerned with the application for increased rates; they had other methods of looking after their transportation problems.
The two central provinces are thickly populated; they are prosperous; they are industrialized to an extent attained by no other province in the dominion. Therefore they were not greatly concerned, and for that reason did not deem it necessary or advisable to argue against the increase, nor indeed to show the slightest interest in it.
I have said that they had other means of taking care of their transportation problem, and I have trucks particularly in mind. They have an organization, largely centred in Ontario, known as the Canadian Automotive Transportation Association, with 5.000 members and employing something like 70,000 persons. They are able therefore to transport goods in certain areas much more efficiently perhaps, and certainly in a manner which gives greater service to the user, than the railways, who depend to a large extent on their long hauls.
I say that Ontario and Quebec, with their population of roughly speaking 7,000,000 people as compared with 1,100,000 in the maritimes, found it hard to appreciate the significance of the increase brought into effect, particularly as Ontario and Quebec were served by this trucking association whose lines extend to every part of these two provinces, doing an exceptionally big business.
I am not criticizing the operations of this organization. They serve a good purpose and I believe in competition. But I repeat that it is because these highly industrialized areas have thickly populated centres that the organizations can operate to the extent that they do.
I noticed in a recent publication an illustration which brings home the points I have in mind, in a comparison between industries in the extreme east and those in the central provinces. I quote:
You know that at Oshawa there is a huge plant manufacturing motor cars and trucks. The axles for these vehicles are made not in Oshawa but in St. Catharines. How do the axles produced on the St. Catharines assembly line flow
smoothly into that main assembly line at Oshawa? Two hundred and forty axles a day have to be delivered. A highway transport company spent weeks working out this problem with officials of the two plants. Four specially designed tractor-trailers were assigned to the run, and a system of carefully scheduled deliveries was evolved. The result is that axles produced at St. Catharines today, Tuesday, will be components of the new cars and trucks rolling off that Oshawa assembly line some time tomorrow.
We find therefore that they are able to give service in Ontario such as we lack in the maritimes. And may I say that whereas this association has connections throughout the central provinces, extending westward, there are no such connections in the maritime provinces. They state definitely that they have no similar organization to carry on their activities in the maritimes.
So you see, Mr. Speaker, that we were concerned about this railway freight rate increase, because we felt that no matter what the increase might be, it would result in a heavier burden on our section of the country than would fall on the two previously mentioned industrial areas.
I pointed out, in my previous remarks on this subject, the background, the early days of the railway system. I referred to confederation, the manner in which Nova Scotia and the maritimes entered it, the undertaking to build the old Intercolonial railway system and to connect Nova Scotia by rail with the industrial areas of central Canada. The measures were designed also to increase the population of the two central provinces, which certainly has been the result, and to industrialize them; but at the same time they would provide a means whereby we should be able to ship our goods into those two large central provinces.
Unfortunately, Mr. Speaker, it has not worked out in that way. It is a long haul from Halifax, we will say, to Toronto, as it is to Montreal and into the larger centres. Unfortunately, manufacturers in the maritimes must bring certain of their products all the way from these industrial centres down to the east coast, and then ship the goods in manufactured form back to the central provinces against keen competition. So I say we have been more or less labouring under a handicap ever since the days of confederation.
The Minister of Transport (Mr. Chevrier) and others may argue that this matter does not enter into the application as presented before the board of transport commissioners and that for this reason they were unable to
Freight Rates

deal with it. I raised that point when I spoke on April 5, and I am going to raise it again today because of the wording of the amended order in council placed before us by the Minister of Transport.
I contend that the reference limited the board of transport commissioners in their findings and deliberations. They dealt with the matter purely from the point of view of dollars and cents and did not take into consideration the spirit of confederation as outlined on many occasions, and as so well set forth by the hon. member for Queens-Lunenburg (Mr. Winters) in his remarks on this subject yesterday. I feel that it is necessary, if we are to bring about a proper adjustment of freight rates, to deal with this subject not only from the point of view of dollars and cents, but also, and more particularly, from the point of view of the spirit of confederation, looking to the development of trade between one section of the country and another. If there is anything in the freight rate structure which is detrimental to any particular section, that structure should be overhauled and a remedy should be found if possible.
Let- me read what I said on April 5 on this question, as reported at page 2641 of Hansard:
Prom my point of view, what is important is the question of trade connections which must be maintained throughout all parts of Canada, and that is a matter which, I suggest to the minister, and through him to the cabinet, should be given serious consideration.
Later in my remarks, as reported in the next column of Hansard, I had something to say along the same lines:
Therefore I say it might be possible for the board of transport commissioners or the government itself to consider whether the whole railway structure should not be revamped so as to bring it more in line with a service to the country such as that given by the postal department.
Again I had in mind the trade of our section of the country with central Canada.
The hon. member for Queens-Lunenburg also touched on maritime freight rates. If I may be permitted to touch on the reasons for what was done in that regard, I should like to do so just briefly. We were not given any preference at that time. It is true that the rate was readjusted and there was an allowance of 20 per cent made to us, but it was not any preference. It was simply a matter of adjustment. At that time, through a review, it was shown and clearly set forth that the index of operations on the old Intercolonial had risen over a period of years to 192-the index being 100, of course-thus showing a 92 point

increase. The index in other sections of the country had increased to only 155, or a 55 point increase. So there was an increase there in the beginning that we must overcome. It was because of the endeavour to equalize the freight rates in all parts of Canada that we in the maritimes were granted an allowance of 20 per cent. Twenty per cent of 192 is 38, and that brings us down to 154 or one cent below the 155, which is no preference so far as we were concerned. We felt at that time that we were simply getting what was rightly ours, and today we are asking for the same consideration, the same attention, that we received on that occasion.
We do not think this 21 per cent increase will result in a horizontally equalized freight rate from one end of Canada to the other. Once again in some cases we shall suffer and be working under a handicap. So as I say, Mr. Speaker, I had hoped that the minister would enlarge the reference which he placed before this house two days later. He brought in a copy of an order in council which in its terms, while asking the board of transport commissioners to look into the over-all structure, did not go as far as I had hoped it would. The orders in council are described in Votes and Proceedings as follows:
Order in council P.C. 1486, approved April 7, 1948: providing that certain tariff schedules authorized by order No. 79425 of the board of transport commissioners for Canada of March 30, 1948, be not interfered with.
Order in council P.C. 1487, approved April 7, 1948: directing the board of transport commissioners for Canada to make a thorough investigation of the rates structure of railways and railway companies which are under the jurisdiction of parliament, with a view to the establishment of a fair and reasonable rates structure which will, under substantially similar circumstances and conditions, be equal in its application to all persons and localities in the various provinces and territories of Canada . . .
When the Minister of Transport spoke yesterday, he did so in an exceptionally fine manner. He is outstanding in that respect, and it is only natural that we followed his remarks with a great deal of interest. In fact I believe the country will read and re-read what the Minister of Transport had to say because his speech contains a great deal of information. Not only did he give us a clear picture of the matters with which the board of transport commissioners have to deal, and the manner in which they must deal with them in making a decision in connection with an application for an increase in rates, but he gave us background material which was most helpful. Then he referred to the powers of the board of transport commissioners, and pointed out that

Freight Rates
the order was sufficiently wide to permit the board to approach the question from all angles.
I am not a lawyer. I am just an ordinary businessman, and certainly would not think of offering my opinion against that of so brilliant a lawyer as the minister. I cannot help believing, however, that there has been a slip in the wording of the minister's order. In some of the judgments the board takes the view that it cannot handle questions relating to trade. Let me place before the house one or two of those judgments. I do not know if I am proceeding in the proper manner in my presentation, but I am sure my legal friends will correct me if I am not doing it properly.
In the case of the application of the District Board of Trade of Coalhurst, Alberta, the finding is stated in these words:
The board under the Railway Act has no profit and loss responsibilities, and its intervention in the matter of rates must, as has been indicated, be concerned with matters falling within the categories of reasonableness and unjust discrimination and not wdth a policy of the development of industries through rate adjustments.
So if we in the maritimes are to gain the point we have in mind, there is question in my mind as to whether the board can deal with the matter in the broad sense I have indicated.
Another quotation states:
The board has no power to regulate tolls for purposes of equalizing costs of production or geographical or climatic or economic conditions.
That was the statement in connection with an application by the Imperial Rice Milling Company vs. the Canadian Pacific Railway Company, case No. 376.
Then there is one other, the British Columbia News Company vs. Express Traffic Association, which reads as follows:
It is not the board's function, as delegated by parliament, to make rates to develop business but to deal with the reasonableness of rates, either on complaint or of its own motion.
Therefore I say one can understand why we in the maritimes and those in other sections of Canada are concerned as to whether the board of transport commissioners will be able to make its finding as full and as broad as we had hoped it would be in a position to make it.
Following the tabling of the order by the Minister of Transport, the hon. member for Rosetown-Biggar (Mr. Coldwell) moved an amendment. I believe I was fair when I stated that the hon. member made a splendid presentation of the matter on April 5; I felt that on that occasion he was fair, and that he created a good impression throughout Canada.
But when he introduced his amendment and was so definite in stating that it was a motion of want of confidence in the government, then I believe he undid all the good he had done. He showed clearly that he was trying to make merely a political manoeuvre, and I feel the hon. member did not do himself justice. Instead of its being a smart move, it rebounded and there has been considerable criticism.

maintopic: FREIGHT RATES-INCREASES ORDERED BY TRANSPORT BOARD-AMENDMENT, MR. COLDWELL- SUBAMENDMENT, MR. BRACKEN
speechtext:
Because of the wording of the amendment offered by the hon. member for Rosetown-Biggar, and his emphasis on the fact that it was a motion of non-confidence- and the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre now reaffirms that fact, and says it was done to put me on the spot-I would say that it was in the true sense a political move which is not in the best interests of the country and does not meet with the wishes or approval of those who, like myself, are sincere in regard to this matter of freight rates.
When that amendment was introduced it gave me a greater opportunity to study what the Minister of Transport had to say. I do not know whether it will take six months or a year to find out what we want to find out. But we do know that so far as the decision of the board of transport commissioners is
Freight Rates

concerned-and I am prepared to accept the words of the Minister of Transport on this point-there was nothing else that the board could do, so far as their reference was concerned. It was simply an application made by the two railway companies of Canada for an increase in freight rates. The board gave consideration to that application and made its finding. That is final. Now, in an effort to assist the east and west, shall I say, the Minister of Transport has broadened his reference and taken a step which I trust will' help my section of the country to readjust matters so that we may be in a better position to compete with industry in central Canada.
I was hoping the minister would have made his reference even broader. I hold in my hand the report of the royal commission on maritime claims, which contains a letter written by the then prime minister to Sir Andrew Rae Duncan, the chairman of that commission. The other members were Hon. W. B. Wallace and Professor Cyrus Macmillan. This letter, dated April 17, 1926, states:
To the Chairman and Members
of the Maritimes Royal Commission: Gentlemen:
The government of Canada is asking you to undertake a task of national importance in inquiring into maritime province grievances. The scope of the inquiry is indicated in the order in council constituting the commission. My colleagues and I desire to emphasize our conviction that the commission should not interpret its instructions or its duties in any narrow or technical sense, but should take every opportunity for the fullest and frankest discussion of the economic difficulties facing this part of the dominion, the endeavours which have been made to overcome them, the causes of any shortcoming in these endeavours, and the most effective and practicable remedies.
The question is not a new one. What is necessary now is to focus the discussion into a practicable program, to take stock of what has been done, of what has been left undone, and of what still may be done.
Then the prime minister of that day went on to refer to our railway problem, the closing paragraph of his letter reading as follows:
I am sure that I am speaking for the people of Canada as a whole when I say that it is our earnest desire that the impartial and thorough inquiry which we anticipate will be made will result in clearing away any misunderstanding or lack of appreciation of one another's problems, and will assist in working out constructive policies for the continued development of the maritime provinces and the welfare of all parts of our common country.
That was signed by the Right Hon. W. L. Mackenzie King, who was then the Prime Minister of Canada. I say to the Minister of Transport that I had hoped he would have found it possible to enlarge his reference to

include the spirit indicated in that letter of the Prime Minister in 1926. I am still hopeful that the minister will show his interest -I know lie has done so already-by allowing this matter to be discussed in the broadest way so that the board of transport commissioners will have the feeling of hon. members from various sections of Canada.
I do not know that they can bring in a satisfactory finding with the present reference. I state again that I am not a legal authority. But there is a difference of opinion. I do feel that the minister has taken a step toward what we have in mind when we ask that the whole railway structure be revamped in the far as it applies to the maritimes will be carried out.
I feel that much good has been done by this discussion. I think the country has a greater understanding of the problems of our railway systems and will appreciate what they are endeavouring to do in the way of providing proper transportation facilities.
As I mentioned in my remarks on April 5, I appreciate, and I think every hon. member who has had any training in business appreciates-I believe the manufacturers, even though they are called upon to pay increased freight rates, recognize this-that you cannot operate a system or any type of business without the necessary revenue. I did not have the report of the Canadian National Railways when I spoke previously, but today I have before me details of the increased cost of the various items which are necessary to carry on a railway system. It is shown clearly that increased revenue must be obtained if they are to get away from the continuing deficits which they had in pre-war days and which they are again showing to the extent of 815,000,000 for the current year.
I am doubtful whether the board of transport commissioners were justified in confining their inquiry to freight rates, which represent 78-2 per cent of the revenue. There is a question whether they should not have considered the over-all picture of the Canadian Pacific and the Canadian National and made a finding on that basis. If they had, I feel sure that the increase would not have been as large as seemed necessary when they were dealing only with one branch of the operations, namely, the freight structure.
I do not apologize for having spoken the second time on this question. I felt it was necessary to do so in view of the additional information supplied to us yesterday by the Minister of Transport in his splendid presentation of the freight rates case. I do not hesitate to stand here in my place or face my

Freight Rates
people. They know how I stand in regard to maritime rights. They know my interest in Nova Scotia. They know that my whole interests are tied up in the development of that particular section of the country. I do not hesitate to stand here today and say that I will not vote for an amendment which is really a vote of no confidence in the government.

He is a fine chap outside the house but when he comes into the house he immediately adopts a political bias which it is hard for me to understand. I would not have dared to say this if the hon. member had not brought it on himself. I say to him in a most kindly way that I am just as sincere in working for Nova Scotia as he is in working for the interests of Vancouver and British Columbia.
It is because of that and the good government which we have had, it is because assistance has been given to Nova Scotia and the maritimes on more than one occasion, that I am not going to vote in favour of a noconfidence motion moved by the leader of the C.C.F. or by any other member of that group.

maintopic: FREIGHT RATES-INCREASES ORDERED BY TRANSPORT BOARD-AMENDMENT, MR. COLDWELL- SUBAMENDMENT, MR. BRACKEN
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, we have listened with a great deal of interest to the remarks of the senior hon. member for Halifax (Mr. Isnor). I agree with much of what he said. First, I agree with his statement that the board in its report did not deal with the subject from the point of view of the spirit of confederation but rather more from the point of view of dollars and cents. That is one of the main objections we from the maritime provinces are taking.
The hon. member also mentioned the fact that he had spoken on this matter before. I also spoke on this matter on a previous occasion and I am not going to apologize for speaking again. I have received a great many letters, telegrams and long distance telephone calls from my own province of New Brunswick. These indicate that people in that part of Canada are still greatly agitated over the freight rates situation. I feel that we are entitled to do all we can to place before the public the true situation of the maritime provinces.
I wish to say at the outset that I am not opposing general increases in rates; after reading the report I feel that increases are necessary. However, what I do question is the method adopted for increasing those rates. I feel that the increase could have been 5849-188
adapted to the situation existing in the various provinces and should have been equally and fairly distributed. I do not think that is the situation.
As I said on April 5 when I spoke before, I consider that we in the maritimes are again being asked to pay more than our full share of the cost and have had placed upon our shoulders more than a full share of this burden.
The senior member for Halifax has given the house something of the history of these freight rates. The history is a long one. Transportation was one of our main problems at the time our province entered confederation, and one of the reasons that induced our province to come in was the assurance given that we would have access to the markets of Canada. From 1867 down to 1912 we were fairly well treated in that regard, because the different governments of Canada allowed the maritime provinces more or less to adjust their own freight rates. But in 1912 a new situation arose. The Intercolonial railway, which was the railway given to the maritime provinces at confederation, was taken over by the Canadian National Railways and in 1912 or 1913 there was an increase of ten per cent in the rates so far as the maritime provinces were concerned. In 1915 there was a further increase of five per cent, and in 1918 another increase of fifteen per cent. For the information of members from other parts of Canada I might point out that the first two of these increases applied only to the maritime provinces, the one in 1912 and the one in 1915. The minister will bear me out in that.

maintopic: FREIGHT RATES-INCREASES ORDERED BY TRANSPORT BOARD-AMENDMENT, MR. COLDWELL- SUBAMENDMENT, MR. BRACKEN
speechtext: I am sorry I was not following the hon. member.

maintopic: FREIGHT RATES-INCREASES ORDERED BY TRANSPORT BOARD-AMENDMENT, MR. COLDWELL- SUBAMENDMENT, MR. BRACKEN
speechtext:
These increases applied only to the maritime provinces, not to the rest of Canada. That is correct. Then in 1918, as I have said, there was another increase of fifteen per cent. All these increases began to put an intolerable burden on the maritime provinces, an increase of many millions of dollars which fell on the shoulders of our people in the maritime provinces and not on the rest of Canada.
In addition it should be pointed out that the maritime provinces have more than borne their share in providing railway extensions for other parts of Canada. When the western provinces were formed, new railways were constructed and the maritime provinces contributed many millions of dollars as their share of that expenditure. So, all in all, our maritime provinces have more than paid their share so far as railway construction and railway freight rates are concerned.
Freight Rates

The situation had become so intolerable in 1925 that all the members of parliament from the maritime provinces joined together in a movement known as "Maritime Rights", in which politics were forgotten so far as the individual members were concerned, all uniting their efforts to remedy the situation. Those efforts resulted in the appointment of the Duncan commission, which investigated the situation and made certain recommendations. I have never felt that those recommendations have been fully implemented. As a matter of fact, when I happened to be, in London, England, a few years ago, I had the honour to meet Sir Andrew Rae Duncan, and he asked me what part of Canada I was from. When I told him I was from the mari-times he said, "You in the maritime provinces are the most long-suffering people there are in Canada, possibly in the whole world. I made certain recommendations in my report but those recommendations have never been fulfilled."
Be that as it may, Mr. Speaker, I am not now discussing those recommendations except the one which has to do with freight rates. The government of that day, 1926, felt that the freight rates problem in the maritimes was a very serious one and that it should receive first consideration, and accordingly it passed in 1927 the Maritime Freight Rates Act. Since then we have been fairly well satisfied with our freight rate structure, but the situation in the maritime provinces has been such that we have not been able to take full advantage of those rates. We all remember that from 1929 to 1938 there was a great depression in this country and business shrank, with the result that the maritime provinces did not have an opportunity to develop manufacturing industry as they would have liked to do. Then from 1939 to 1945 we passed through a second world war, during which the maritime provinces had no opportunity of developing the industries they would have liked to develop.
In 1947 and 1948, when possibly we could have made some advances, we find ourselves handicapped by the imposition of these increased freight rates, a horizontal increase of 21 per cent on all our industries in the maritimes. To show that these increases are having a very serious effect in the maritime provinces, I should like to quote a paragraph or two from a telegram that was sent to the Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King) on April 9 last by the chairman of the transportation commission of the Maritime Board of Trade. For the information of hon. members, the commission is composed of men chosen from every political party in the maritime 
provinces, outstanding men chosen for their knowledge of railway matters and economics, and whose judgment is considered sound. They are men who are not easily alarmed. This is what the chairman of the transportation commission said in his telegram to the Prime Minister:
You as the head of the then government-
He was speaking of the government in 1926. -authorized the hearings of the Sir Andrew Rae Duncan commission which recommended the present Maritime Freight Rates Act. In the opinion of this commission the spirit and terms of this act have been violated and in addition to that the imposition of an horizontal twenty-one per cent increase in freight rates means that maritime industry in many cases will be seriously affected and in some cases destroyed.
That is pretty strong language and, as I say, it comes from men who are not alarmists but men of good sound business judgment in the maritime provinces. The telegram goes on to say:
This is not only true in regard to industry but it applies with equal force to agriculture.
The telegram is a long one but that is all I shall quote at the moment.
I should like to point out that as to the judgment of the board of transport commissioners, counsel who represented the maritime transportation commission expressed the opinion that the spirit and terms of the Maritime Freight Rates Act had been violated. It was also pointed out that no recognition was givm to the strong contention of the maritimes that in the event increases were found necessary the board, under the Railway Act, had power itself to exempt or provide limitations to percentage increases. The board itself in its judgment on page 43 has this to say:
For the maritime provinces it is essential that they continue to find, to a considerable degree, markets for their primary products, as well as their manufactured products, in the more densely populated areas of the provinces of Quebec and Ontario, where competition is keen. The number of manufacturing industries in New Brunswick and Nova Scotia is not large, but they are of much importance to the areas concerned. In spite of the distance from the markets to be found in the large centres they have, rvith, perhaps, one or two exceptions, managed to overcome largely their geographical disadvantage and make progress. For these industries concern is expressed lest they be put at a disadvantage with their competitors, in the event that a horizontal increase in freight rates such as applied for is allowed.
I might say that nothing was done about this. What I have read is part of the judgment of the board that was studying this matter.
The question arises as to whether these freight rates in any way affect our industries in the maritime provinces. Mr. Rand Matheson,

Freight Rates
who is secretary of the maritime transportation commission, has made a study of the question. He found, for instance, that on hard woods from Antigonish to Toronto there will be an increase of $2.80 per 1,000 feet. With competition such as that, I ask this house, how is it possible for these people in Antigonish to compete with industries in Ontario and Quebec? He estimates that on apples from Kentville, Nova Scotia, to Toronto the increase will be twenty-seven cents a barrel.
When I was speaking on this matter a few days ago I pointed out that the Annapolis valley of Nova Scotia, in the past, under the empire trade agreements, had an opportunity of sending its apples to Great Britain; as a matter of fact, I think 90 per cent of the pick of the apples in the Annapolis valley was shipped overseas. These apples must now find markets in central Canada and1 in other parts of Canada. In order that they may be shipped to central Canada, they will have to meet an increase of twenty-seven cents a barrel in freight rates. He also spoke about feed grains. It has been announced in the house that the assistance to feed grains will be continued as before, and I wish to thank the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Gardiner) for this and assure him that it will be of great benefit to the farmers in the maritime provinces.
Sixty thousand tons of fertilizer are used in New Brunswick alone. To a great extent this fertilizer comes from Hamilton, Ontario, and from other parts of Ontario. The increase in freight on fertilizer is $1.40 a ton, which will increase the cost of producing potatoes and other farm produce in New Brunswick. Mr. Matheson says that potatoes from Charlottetown, Prince Edward Island, and Grand Falls, New Brunswick, will be increased six cents a 75-pound bag. Besides having to pay the extra cost of fertilizer, farm machinery and everything else that goes into the production in the maritimes, we shall also have to pay the extra amount of freight and still try to compete with the farmers of Quebec and Ontario. Frozen fish from Halifax and Saint John to Winnipeg will be increased thirty-one cents per 100 pounds. Steel sheet for manufacturing, shipped from Hamilton, Ontario to Sackville, New Brunswick, will be increased by $2.40 a ton. I might point out that in Sackville, New Brunswick, a very high grade of stove is manufactured. These people have been able to compete in the past with like articles all across Canada. With this increase in the material coming from Ontario to the maritimes, and then again the increase in
freight rates from the maritimes to the different markets, it will be almost prohibitive for this industry and many other similar industries in these provinces.
Mr. Matheson also analysed the difference in first-class and fifth-class freight rates per 100 pounds. He points out that on the first-class rate from Halifax and Saint John to Windsor, Ontario, there is an increase of four cents per 100 pounds over the difference established by the Maritime Freight Rates Act. He points out that iwe are not getting the benefit of the Maritime Freight Rates Act, and that this is a violation of that act.
When I spoke before I think I mentioned the fact that $8,000,000 will probably be the amount that the maritime provinces will have to pay out of the $70,000,000 which will be received from the increase. The senior member for Halifax mentioned it today. In the maritimes we have a population of about one million people. There are approximately thirteen million people in Canada. We are paying $8,000,000. If we paid our proper proportion, and everything else was equal, we would be paying one-thirteenth of the cost of this increase instead of just a little over eight per cent.
I should like to refer to another industry in New Brunswick which has been giving, perhaps more than any other, considerable concern. I refer to the coal industry. The coal industry in New Brunswick is not a great industry when compared with the same industry in other parts of Canada. As a matter of fact it is a small industry when compared with the great industry of Nova Scotia and of Alberta and of other sections. But to us in New Brunswick it is a very important-industry. As a matter of fact the whole economy of our province is more or less bound up in the coal industry around Minto and Chipman in our province. We get our hydro electric development from the production of coal. Our pulp and paper mills use our coal, and there is a splendid market right in our own province for the coal production if we were not interfered with from the outside. I should like to point out to the Minister of Transport (Mr. Chevrier) just how we are interfered with so far as coal is concerned. I have mentioned it in this house on previous occasions. On Nova Scotia coal which is shipped out of that province there are what are known as subventions. These subventions are paid on coal shipped by that province to Ontario and Quebec and also to New Brunswick to the extent that Nova Scotia coal can be shipped into New Brunswick and delivered at
Freight Rates

points such as Bathurst, Newcastle, Chatham, Dalhousie and to other industrial centres at a lower rate or at the same rate as is paid for New Brunswick coal. The result of that competition is very unfair, and it has made it very difficult indeed for the New Brunswick coal operators and coal mines to carry on.
Just the other day the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Howe.) assured the hon. member for Cape Breton South (Mr. Gillis) that in any increase in the freight rates as far as Nova Scotia coal was concerned there would be a corresponding increase in the subventions. This will make a more serious situation in our province because, as I mentioned a moment ago, no subventions are paid for New Brunswick coal which is being shipped in the province itself, where most of our coal is consumed. The result will be that the competition, which has been very severe in the past, will be more severe than ever.
In that connection I should like to read some telegrams I have received from the mining industry in the province. The first one is dated Minto, April 21:
If the freight rate increase authorized by the board of transport commissioners is allowed to remain in force the coal mining industry upon which this community depends will suffer most seriously. Some time ago we gave you information showing the serious financial and competitive position in which this industry has been placed. The direct result of this increase will be to make that position very much worse. Indirectly this industry will suffer because of the general curtailing effect upon all New Brunswick industries. In view of this most critical situation every New Brunswick member has a most serious responsibility placed upon him, also a great opportunity to give vital service to his province. We urge you therefore to use all your influence to protect the interests of this community and this province by having removed this unjust and unequal burden which has been placed upon us.
That is signed by the Minto chamber of commerce. There is a further telegram from the same community addressed to myself:
This New Brunswick coal mining industry has for a long time been suffering from discriminatory freight rates. The present increase will make the situation worse. The announced increase in subventions to the central provinces will not help us as our market is nearly all within New Brunswick. Because of this our percentage increase will be higher than the average. In one of the worst instances the rate jumped from 30 cents to 55 cents per ton on a haul of three to ten miles. Coal mining will also suffer because all New Brunswick industry will be given a severe set back. We are looking to you to stand firmly for the rights of this province and to do everything possible to protect this industry.

This is from the New Brunswick coal producers association. The minister may tell me that there has been a five cent reduction in the twenty-five cents per ton on coal moving in the maritimes.

The long hauls between Vancouver and Montreal will be the ones that take the

brunt of it, and the ones from Montreal east. What I should like to see is that the board of transport commissioners, before they arrive at their decision, take this matter into consideration and that the loss, if any, be suffered by the consolidated revenue fund of Canada.
Some mention has been made of the seven provinces which have made representations with a view to having the board's decision held up for thirty days. This has been a bone of contention for the last couple of weeks or so. Great emphasis has been laid on the benefit which would be derived from holding up the matter for thirty days. For my part, while I believe it might possibly have been better if that had been done, at the same time there is no object in doing so, from the very fact that the board of transport commissioners have now been given instructions to go ahead. The provinces have the chance to appeal. If they are right, they have the same opportunity as they had before.
The main freight hauling from western Canada to the east is in connection with grain. That matter has not been touched at all. Naturally western Canada is looking to eastern Canada for a market for its feed grain. The federal government is paying a subsidy on this feed grain moving east, and the amount of that subsidy is coming out of the consolidated revenue fund. This subsidy is helping to market our feed grain in eastern Canada. Because of the climate in eastern Canada it is far more convenient to feed stock there than it is in the western provinces.
I do not know whether I have been rightly or wrongly informed, but I have been given some information about the competition between the Canadian Pacific, a privately owned railway, and the Canadian National Railways, which is nationally owned. My information is that the effect of an order of the board of transport commissioners is that the Canadian National is not allowed to compete unfairly with the Canadian Pacific. I am informed that a train on the nationally owned line can travel from Vancouver to Montreal in about nine or ten hours less time but, because of the hampering restriction of the board of transport commissioners in curtailing speed, they are not allowed to compete in that way.
I believe that is one reason why trains of the Canadian National are running only half filled with passengers, while those of the Canadian Pacific are filled. This is the condition, despite the fact that the Canadian National track is straighter, their grade is lower, they use only one engine between Montreal and Vancouver and, if pressure were put on the board of transport commissioners or
those who are in charge of the travel of these trains, they could make much faster time and still travel at a safe speed. I understand that the time between Winnipeg and Ottawa could be cut by seven hours. I believe that with these changes the revenues of the Canadian National would increase considerably. As I said before, I am voting with the government.

maintopic: FREIGHT RATES-INCREASES ORDERED BY TRANSPORT BOARD-AMENDMENT, MR. COLDWELL- SUBAMENDMENT, MR. BRACKEN
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, in this debate on the subject of freight rates let me at the outset advance the point of view that this is a national problem, one of concern to the whole of Canada and, therefore, properly to be discussed in the House of Commons. At the same time I agree with the hon. member who has just taken his seat that there should be no controversy between east and west, or between the central provinces and the east and west. There should be no controversy; but we have to deal with actualities, and there will be controversy so long as the extremes of the country are at a disadvantage in this particular matter as compared with the central part. That being so, and the hon. member holding the belief he expressed as to the desirability of doing away with controversy, I suggest that he join with us in attempting to remove the causes of that controversy. That is what we are doing when we seek to have an equalization of freight rates as between British Columbia and the maritime provinces, and central Canada.
I do not intend to enter into a controversy as to who is actually most prejudiced by the present freight rates structure, whether it be the maritimes, the prairies or British Columbia. But I do wish to place before the house some of the rates in existence, so that hon. members may judge whether we in British Columbia are prejudiced.
In this connection I would quote from the judgment of commissioner MacPherson as it appears at pages 84 and 85 of the judgments of the board of transport commissioners for Canada. Referring at the outset of his judgment to the mountain differential, Mr. MacPherson says this:
During the progress of the hearing it was pointed out by counsel for the provinces on many occasions that in Canada we have different grades or steps in the freight rate structure, viz.,
The maritime rates (in preferred territory)
The competitive rates of Ontario and Quebec
Freight Rates

The prairie rates for Manitoba, Saskatchewan, and Alberta
The mountain scale or Pacific scale of rates.
Then he went on to say at page 85:
Then lastly there is the mountain or Pacific scale which is commonly referred to as mountain differential, whereby one and one-quarter prairie miles equal one mile in Pacific territory for rate purposes. I am of the opinion that this situation, which amounts to an increase of sixteen per cent over the prairie scale of rates, should be again reviewed at the earliest possible date.
By inference the commission is there agreeing with those who claim that on account of the mountain differential, which means an increase of sixteen per cent over the prairie rate which, in turn, is higher than, the rate in central Canada, we in British Columbia are hardest hit by the freight rates structure. So that the importance of this question to British Columbia can be seen, by reference to the judgment of the commissioner. We from British Columbia would ask the co-operation of all members in the house at this time to remove that differential, the cause of our grievance.
It has been said, and clearly proven, that the railway problem in Canada is a national one. The railways were constructed as part of a national policy in the building of Canada so as to ensure that our lines of communication, trade and commerce should be east and west, rather than north and south. That policy has carried with it certain benefits as well as some difficulties. But inasmuch as the whole of Canada has participated in the benefits, it stands to reason that the whole of Canada should be concerned about removing the disadvantages. Since it is a national policy it follows, also, that both the welfare of the railways which serve the national interest, and the welfare of the country in its relationship to the railways are matters of national concern, and should be discussed in parliament.
It follows from this reasoning that the welfare of British Columbia, as part of Canada, is also an item for consideration in this house. At this point I should like to deal with the argument advanced yesterday by the Minister of Transport (Mr. Chevrier) that the board of transport commissioners was justified in concluding that an increase in freight rates was necessary, and at the same time in making an award, without removing the discriminatory features in our freight rate structure.
During the course of my argument today I do not intend to question that some increase in revenue on the part of the railways is necessary. That fact I take for granted because, after all, after fourteen months of hearings the board has come to that conclusion. Certainly I would not question it, and I doubt

if anyone who has participated in the debate would question it. However, what I am concerned about is the minister's statement that the board was justified in awarding the increase without at the same time taking any steps to remove the discrimination.
It must be admitted that at that time the board concerned itself only with a revenue case. The minister himself said that, when at page 2898 of Hansard he is reported to have said:
The board dealt with and was faced purely with a revenue case.
I do not, however, accept the suggestion that there was no other issue before the board. I maintain that there was the issue of discrimination under the freight rates structure; and that aspect of the matter I would ask leave to deal with later.
I agree with the minister when he says that the main consideration before the board was the revenue aspect of the case, and also when he says that, in making its decision the board did not allow itself to give consideration to political or economic questions outside the matter of revenue. But I submit that political or economic questions, in the broadest sense of those terms, must be considered in arriving at any fair decision with regard to what freight rates may be found to be necessary. I say that is a national problem, and I submit that, therefore, the government of Canada must be concerned with the political and economic implications of the question and that the Canadian House of Commons is the proper place in which to make our views known to the government.
I have no criticism to' make of the railroads for applying for a rate increase, or of the board for deciding that an increase was necessary. But we have the strongest criticism to make of the government for allowing the increase to go into effect without removing the inequalities under which various sections of this country have suffered for years. That is the point involved in the first paragraph of the amendment moved by the leader of the opposition (Mr. Bracken), and I should like to read this paragraph in order to bring out that aspect of the situation. It reads:
That all the words after "this house" in the fourth line of the amendment be deleted, and that the following be substituted instead thereof:
"Regrets the government's failure to secure the removal of inequalities and discriminations in the Canadian railway freight rates structure before the imposition of a horizontal increase of twenty-one per cent-an increase which is bound to intensify the aforesaid inequalities and discriminations."

Freight Rates
That first paragraph of the amendment indicates the clear issue which is being placed before this House of Commons for consideration. In connection with that point I ask hon. members to consider the effect of this 21 per cent increase upon the economy of British Columbia. For this purpose I should like to divide our population into three groups. The first group would be made up of consumers generally. We are all consumers and, therefore, we are all affected by an increase in freight rates. It has not been denied and it cannot be denied that, since we already have a tremendous differential, a greater burden will be imposed upon our province than upon the rest of Canada. An increase of 21 per cent all across the board hits us that much harder. Therefore the consumer in British Columbia will be that much harder hit than the consumer anywhere else. As an example of this fact I should like to refer to a report in the Winnipeg Free Press of April 10, reading as follows:
Freight Rate Compensation Shortening and soap will rise in price
Ottawa, April 10-The wartime prices and trade board will shortly authorize increases in the prices of shortening and soap to compensate for the increases in freight rates, it was learned Friday.
There we see the beginning of the increase in the cost of living which affects our consumer population in British Columbia much more adversely than the consumers in the rest of Canada.
The second classification I should like to make for this purpose is made up of our farmers. The province, particularly the interior from which I come, is interested principally in the primary industries of farming and logging. These primary producers will be affected because they must pay the increase both on the things they have to buy and on the things they have to sell. It has been said, and said truly, that the farmer is the only person whose costs are doubly affected by any increase in freight rates. Certainly that is true of the livestock industry where you have to ship your cattle. It is always the case that from the return received from the sale of cattle there is deducted the amount of freight from the collection point to the marketing point, which in our case is Vancouver, Calgary or Edmonton. Not only is the farmer hurt because of the increase he must pay on everything he has to buy, but he will have this extra freight deducted from the prices of the things he has to sell.
The president of the tree fruits industry in British Columbia, Mr. Lloyd, has already said -this was referred to last night by the hon.
member for Vancouver South (Mr. Green)- that this increase in freight rates will cost the British Columbia fruit industry approximately SI.COO,000 a year. The effect of this increase will be that much greater on our people.
The third category which I should like to consider is made up of the railway employees themselves. In British Columbia they are concerned both as consumers and as railway workers. In many areas in the interior the prosperity of the district is largely dependent upon the prosperity and stability of employment enjoyed by the railway worker. I am quite certain that no railway employee in British Columbia, facing this problem as he must as a British Columbian, as a consumer and as a railway worker, wants any increase in freight rates to be made at the expense of our province or indeed at the expense of any section of Canada. I have spoken to some representatives of the railway employees, and they are as vitally interested as anyone else in the removal of discriminations in connection with freight rates.
I maintain that the wage increases which the railway employees are asking for should form no part of this discussion. We must not allow the wage requirements of the railroads and their employees to be caught in the cross fire of political controversy. One or two addresses which have been delivered in this debate have indicated a tendency toward making this aspect of the matter a political issue. I want to make it clear that I am not opposed to any increases in freight rates as such, but I am opposed to increases without equalization, to increases which increase discrimination at the expense of the railway workers, quite as much as that of anyone else in British Columbia.
In order to keep the record clear in this respect, I should like to refer to what the leader of the opposition said yesterday. He indicated clearly that he felt the position of the railway workers should not be prejudiced as a result of this discussion. The leader of the opposition said, as reported on page 2911 of Hansard of April 13:
Roughly it would appear that they have received on an average about twenty-five cents an hour increase. But the cost of living, as compared with pre-war days, has gone up 50 per cent, while the average wages of railway employees it would appear have gone up only some 33 per cent.
And then again on the same page:
These working men and women have had no adjustment of wage rates since June of 1946. Yet since that date the cost of living index has risen 27-2 points over the 1938-39 average, and the food index has gone up 43-8 points during
Freight Rates

Pacific scale of rates is higher than other scales of rates, such as the prairie scale. This condition, it is alleged, works to the serious disadvantage of the business and industries of British Columbia, and is most discriminatory in respect to that province. It is further submitted that this situation should be taken fully into account by the board in fixing rates in the present case. The submissions of British Columbia on this subject had the full support of a number of witnesses in Alberta.
Some other questions raised in the submissions made during the western hearings had to do with rates to assist and develop industry.
Farther on he says:
Wide latitude was given to the protestants in the development of their objections to the proposed increase.
Then he goes on to show that in fact they had all raised this question of discrimination; therefore the question was certainly before the board. The minister has taken two completely different positions. On the one hand he says, as reported on page 2907 of Hansard, that the matter was not. before the board; that the only thing properly before the board was the question of the revenue situation. On the other hand he says in the same speech that the board of transport commissioners themselves said that there was nothing in the Railway Act which hampered them in any way in dealing with the inequalities of the so-called discrimination which may exist in this country.

speechtext: The minister has made that point before. Counsel for the provinces said that if we were making at the moment an application for the removal of discrimination it would be brought out and that we would have to make separate submissions. Their position was: This application was made by the railway company. We admit that they are not applying for the removal of discrimination, but an integral part of our position was that it could not and should not be granted without at the same time removing discrimination. Therefore the point I make is that there could be, in my view, no doubt that the question of discrimination was very much before the board during the whole course of this hearing.

speechtext: I do not agree with the hon. gentleman.

maintopic: FREIGHT RATES-INCREASES ORDERED BY TRANSPORT BOARD-AMENDMENT, MR. COLDWELL- SUBAMENDMENT, MR. BRACKEN
speechtext:
The fact that they declined to take action on it is a matter, the reasons for which can be known only to them, but there was nothing to prevent them at that time from taking action to deal with the inequalities and discrimination in the Canadian freight rate structure. That being the case, it seems to me that the government has been compelled further to reverse its position. Immediately after the freight rates decision was made known, seven of the provinces said that they would apply for a stay in its imposition. The government refused to grant that stay. They concurred in the immediate imposition of the freight rates increase. I wish to make this clear. The government concurred in the imposition of the new freight rates, and the western provinces, of course, took that as an insult. In fact one is given to understand that in some of their minds it was taken as being an indication that the governor in council did not propose to permit them to make an appeal from the decision. We now find that the government is saying, While we will go ahead with the imposition of the freight rates immediately, we shall have to allow the provinces to appeal the actual award. The present decision of the government followed the protest which was raised in the house as soon as an opportunity was given to discuss the matter of freight rates, the protest which took place on Monday, April 5, and again on Wednesday, April 7, a protest which was joined in vigorously, in fact

Freight Rates
almost led by members from British Columbia, including members on the government side.
May I at this point read some of the submissions made by the provincial premiers, tabled in the house yesterday by the minister. The Premier of Alberta said this:
The decision of the board of transport commissioners authorizing an over-all increase of 21 per cent in freight rates has been a shock and a severe disappointment to the people of Alberta. This province has for many years suffered from excessive and discriminatory freight rates and the judgment of the transport commissioners only serves to aggravate that situation. This province desires and intends to appeal from the board's decision to the governor general in council. If increased' rates made effective now and then the governor in council as we confidently expect rescinds the board's increase order much confusion and dislocation of business will inevitably result. The government of Alberta respectfully requests the governor in council to use the power conferred by section 52 of the Railway 4.ct and vary the transport board's order 70425 jy extending three days notice period to thirty lays.
The Premier of Saskatchewan made a similar submission. The province of British Columbia wired in the following terms:
Government of British Columbia protests strongly any increase in freight rates under recent ruling of board of transport until such time as the mountain differential affecting British Columbia and Alberta is removed. Existence of mountain differential constitutes a grave injustice under ordinary circumstances. Imposition of a 21 per cent increase in freight rates would further accentuate the injustice and place both British Columbia and Alberta in very disadvantageous positions within Canada's economy. Strongly urge that ruling of board of transport commissioners be withheld from operation until such time as British Columbia government has opportunity to appeal against the decision.
Byron I. Johnson, Premier of British Columbia.
These requests from the premiers of the seven provinces were, as the house knows, in effect rejected by the dominion government which introduced the order in council referred to yesterday, saying that the governor in council had considered the representations and had come to the conclusion that the freight increases must be granted forthwith.
Then, as I say, there was a protest which took place in the house, in which western members on all sides joined, and the government then reversed or partly reversed its decision and said, "We will continue to make the increase effective as of now but will permit an appeal and will in fact refer the matter of discrimination to the board."
The point is this. The question of discrimination was before the board. The government has the power to insist that discrimination be removed, and I suggest that it should
have done so at the outset and not waited until the protests in the house and in the country became so great that the government was forced to throw out the sop that it would submit the matter to the board, at the same time forcing itself to say that such consideration would take from six months to a year before any effective action could be taken.
In conclusion, Mr. Speaker, I wish to read from an editorial that appeared in the Vancouver Sun of April 9, 1948, which sums up the position we take:
This government has been in power since 1935. At any time since then, if it was sincerely concerned about the inequalities in the national freight rate structure, it could have instructed the transport board to make a revision. But no. The government thought it politically unwise to arouse the animosity of Quebec and Ontario, hereditary beneficiaries of the obsolete system.
Only at this late date, when the chickens of neglect have come home to roost on Parliament Hill, does the government decide "it would be in the public interest to have a thorough investigation . . . with' a view to the establishment of a fair and reasonable rate structure."
There is absolutely no evidence that such an inquiry would have been started by Ottawa on its own volition. If the railroads had not asked for a percentage boost across the board, and won their case before the transport commissioners, the government would have been quite content to continue its neglect.
This government has given the victims of regional rate discrimination not the slightest grounds to believe that it is interested in inequalities as such. It is interested, however, in shutting up the roars of protest evoked by a 21 per cent magnification of the injustices.
The editorial concludes with these words:
A test of how genuine is Ottawa's sudden conversion would be an application to the government for subsidies on B.C.'s freight bills pending the transport board's rulings.
This would give Ottawa a cash reason for speeding up the hearings. B.C. business is genuinely alarmed at transport minister Chevrier's estimate of one or two years for the investigation. A restriction of that duration on B.C.'s trade with the prairies would be intolerable.
