maintopic: FREIGHT RATES-INCREASES ORDERED BY TRANSPORT BOARD-AMENDMENT, MR. COLD WELL   SUBAMENDMENT, MR. BRACKEN
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, this is the second time we are debating freight rates in that many weeks, and it may be useful to state at this time the reason for this type of procedure. I think the public generally knows that on October 9, 1946, the railway association applied for an increase in freight rates, and immediately after that application was made opposition was taken to it by various provincial governments and members of this house. Many of them would like to have debated that issue in the intervening time between the application and the decision, but were prevented
[Mr. St. Laurent.J
from doing so because of the rules of the house, which preclude our debating any matter which is before a judicial body.
I think it will be admitted also that, after the announcement of the board was made on March 30, the hon. member for Rosetown-Biggar (Mr. Coldwell), when he rose on April 5 and asked that this house debate the question, was doing a public service to the people who are interested in this issue, both in eastern and in western Canada.
It is possible that, had not the hon. member risen at that time and initiated a debate on this very important issue, the decision might have been accepted without very much protest in this house, and the people concerned would not have had the benefit of what I consider to have been an interesting and valuable debate here.
The second motion which the hon. member for Rosetown-Biggar made came on April 7, which followed the statement made by the Minister of Transport (Mr. Chevrier) in reply to the debate of April 5. The motion was necessary because the statement the minister made on April 7 in this house was not satisfactory either to the members of the house or to the provincial governments concerned.
The minister, in his remarks yesterday, made some statements with which we can agree, but which he was not exactly in a position to make, because he is reported on April 13 to have said, at page 2908 of Hansard,-.
Any hon. member who attempts to make a political issue out of this question is to my mind doing a disservice, not only to himself bait to his country.
I agree with that statement, but I think it is clear, from reading all the debates in the house, that when the hon. member for Rosetown-Biggar raised the question in the house in the first instance, and again on the second occasion, it was not on a political basis. As a matter of fact, the hon. member for Fraser Valley (Mr. Cruickshank), who spoke in that debate, made the statement in this house, complimenting the hon. member for Rosetown-Biggar, that he had left politics entirely out of the matter and was to be commended therefor. So that the debate which was initiated in this house started off on a very reasonable basis; but before the Minister of Transport had finished his speech, he himself had introduced certain political considerations into the question.

Freight Rates
For example, he made what amounted to an accusation, that there was some type of lobbying going on from the province of Saskatchewan. He said, in reply to a statement of the hon. member for Rosetown-Biggar:
I have realized that since this debate started, because no one has been flooded with more telegrams than I have from members of the province of Saskatchewan. And this indicates to me that there is some attempt to make a political issue out of this question.
That statement was unfair, and it was inaccurate because, as a matter of fact, the members of this house who represent the constituencies which are affected by this increase have all been receiving telegrams, resolutions and letters which have been urging us to make our views heard in this house. For example, coming from Manitoba, I have a resolution which comes from a municipal council in that province. It happens to come from the rural municipality of Dauphin. The resolution is in these words:
Whereas the board of transport commissioners authorized an increase of 21 per cent in railway freight rates.
And whereas the said increase will bring about an increase in price on all commodities detrimental to our economy and cause inflation.
Now therefore be it resolved that we protest against the proposed increase in freight rates until an equality in way freight rates has been established as between eastern Canada and the prairie provinces.
That is a resolution which is characteristic of the type of resolutions and telegrams we have been receiving. They have been coming not only from municipal bodies but from locals of pool elevators, co-operatives of different kinds, boards of trade and so on. They have been coming from other provinces as well as from Saskatchewan. Therefore I do not know that the minister was on solid ground when he intimated that Saskatchewan exclusively was carrying on a lobby on this question.
As a matter of fact, a statement was made here the other day to the effect that it is quite possible that the hon. member for Rosthern (Mr. Tucker) who, I understand is in Saskatchewan at the present time, may be doing his quota of lobbying on this question. He is reported in the western papers to have stated that in his opinion the western provinces-that is, the prairie provinces-will get a square deal out of this decision yet; that the announcement of the board of transport commissioners is not final; that it is in the nature of an advisory ruling, and that the government will see to it that an equalization is carried out. Of course that hope is somewhat on a par with his ill-fated hope on the coarse grains issue. It is too bad that he has not had an opportunity to state his views in the house during this debate. The hon. member for Rosthern seems to have the uncanny faculty of being in Saskatchewan when the issues are hot in Ottawa and of being in Ottawa when they are hot in Saskatchewan.
I think it can be said, however, that for the most part the members who took part in this debate have shown something which is perhaps new on this issue, and that is an awareness that our transportation system in this country has graduated from being a purely commercial undertaking, and is now a social undertaking. I believe there is a new realization, perhaps brought about by events in recent years, that the transportation system of this country is now so vitally necessary to all provinces and to all people concerned that we can no longer treat it as a purely commercial operation requiring so much revenue to provide certain services, and leave it at that. We must take into consideration the burden of keeping that transportation system functioning and giving good service in parts of Canada which in themselves may not be able to produce the necessary revenue. It might be considered perhaps as a minor version of the situation we have in our post office system. Our post office system takes into consideration the convenience and necessity of communication for the country as a whole. Where it is found necessary to give service to a certain community, that service is given regardless of whether or not it is possible to raise in that district the revenue with which to pay for the service. Something of that kind of consideration must now be taken into account in dealing with this question of freight rates.
There are, of course, two broad phases involved. The first is the general flat increase of 21 per cent, and the second is the discrimination as a result of the differentials that exist. On the first issue-that is, on the general increase-I believe it is in a way one of the fruits of the government's decontrol policy. The government were warned on more than one occasion that, if they continued their decontrol policy, they would be

faced with one problem after another; and this freight rate problem is not the last one. There will be other problems along the same lines and emanating from the same reasons. The other day the minister stated that the cost of operating railways, the level of wages and the expense of maintaining our system have increased. That is true. But the government itself will have to take the responsibility for having permitted prices to rise to the point where it was necessary for the men working in this industry to ask for higher wages. I do not think that one member of this house has
said a word in opposition to the efforts being made by the railroad workers to have their wages increased, because we realize that the cost of living today is such that it is necessary for them to ask for that increase.
It is not possible for me to complete my remarks, Mr. Speaker, so I would move the adjournment of the debate.
On motion of Mr. Zaplitny the debate was adjourned.
At six o'clock the house adjourned, without question put, pursuant to standing order.
